content: This review is part of a series that evaluates various methods for cervical ripening and induction of labor using standardized methodologies. The objective of this specific review was to assess the effects of extra-amniotic prostaglandins for cervical ripening or labor induction during the third trimester of pregnancy. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of June 2009) and reviewed bibliographies of relevant studies. They included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared the use of extra-amniotic prostaglandins for cervical ripening or labor induction with either placebo, no treatment, or other predefined methods of labor induction. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies and extracted data. A total of 12 studies were included in the review. Among the primary outcomes, it was found that significantly fewer women achieved vaginal delivery within 24 hours when labor was induced with extra-amniotic prostaglandin F2 alpha compared to vaginal misoprostol (risk ratio [RR] 2.43; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.42 to 4.15). No other statistically significant differences in primary outcomes were observed between the groups. The use of oxytocin to initiate or augment labor was significantly less frequent when extra-amniotic prostaglandins were compared to placebo (RR 0.51; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.67). However, oxytocin use was significantly more frequent when extra-amniotic prostaglandins were compared to vaginal misoprostol (RR 1.73; 95% CI 1.20 to 2.49). When extra-amniotic prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) was compared to the use of a Foley catheter alone, the only notable difference was a lower incidence of an unfavorable cervix 12 to 24 hours after treatment in the prostaglandin group (RR 0.59; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.86). Women who received extra-amniotic prostaglandins reported higher satisfaction with the treatment (mean difference 4.40; 95% CI 3.50 to 5.30) and were less likely to feel embarrassed compared to those treated with vaginal PGE2 (RR 8.91; 95% CI 2.26 to 35.02). No other significant differences were observed when extra-amniotic prostaglandins were compared with other methods of cervical ripening or labor induction. Although these findings suggest that extra-amniotic prostaglandins may be as effective as other agents for labor induction, the results are difficult to interpret due to the small sample sizes and limited statistical power of the included studies. Most comparisons showed no significant differences, and the confidence intervals were wide. The authors concluded that the evidence from this review is limited by the small sample sizes and the division of participants into multiple comparison groups. While extra-amniotic prostaglandins may be as effective as other methods for initiating labor, there is insufficient conclusive evidence to guide clinical practice. A well-designed, adequately powered randomized controlled trial is needed to determine whether the use of extra-amniotic prostaglandins could reduce the rate of cesarean sections.
